name: Blueberry
summary: Blueberry is rare in the Philippines: there are no blueberry farms, only wild native blueberries such as ayusip in the Benguet mountains, now being raised in plots to save them, and a few hobby growers with imported bushes in pots in Baguio and other cool highland towns. This short guide covers how those few growers keep them alive, which comes down to cool air and very sour soil.
season: Plants are set out at the start of the rains, about May to July, in the highlands. Bushes flower and fruit in the cool, drier months. Wild ayusip fruits in the mountains in season and is picked by locals and hikers.
material: Nursery plants in pots, either imported low chill bush types or rooted cuttings, or native ayusip raised from cuttings. Plants are moved with a full ball of soil around the roots. Bare root plants bear less.
spacing: About 1 to 1.5 m between bushes in beds, or one bush to a large pot. At least two types near each other for pollination.
water: Kept evenly damp with rain water where possible. The shallow roots dry out fast and also rot in standing water.
fertilizer: Pine needle compost and mulch, small amounts of ammonium sulfate (21 0 0). No lime, no ash, no fresh manure.
care: Pine needle mulch, steady watering, removing first year flowers, pruning old canes after fruiting, netting against birds.
harvest: Berries are picked a few days after turning fully blue, by hand, into shallow containers, and eaten or sold fresh within days. Wild ayusip is gathered in the mountains in small amounts.

ways.label: Potted plants (punla sa paso)

steps.title: Make very sour soil
steps.how: Blueberries need soil far more sour than most crops, about pH 4.5 to 5.5. Highland growers fill big pots or raised beds with composted pine needles, pine bark, rotted leaves and a little garden soil.

steps.title: Plant with the soil ball whole
steps.how: Set each plant at the same depth it grew, keeping the soil ball unbroken, about 1 to 1.5 m apart, and plant at least two types together so they pollinate each other. Mulch thickly with pine needles.

steps.title: Water with soft water
steps.how: Keep the soil evenly damp, never dry and never soggy. Rain water is best, since hard tap water slowly makes the soil less sour.

steps.title: Feed lightly with sour feeds
steps.how: Top up the pine needle mulch and feed small amounts of ammonium sulfate (21 0 0) or acid compost now and then. Skip lime, ash and fresh manure.

steps.title: Prune out old canes
steps.how: Pinch off flowers in the first year so the bush grows. From the second year, cut out weak, dead and very old canes after fruiting.

steps.title: Pick fully blue berries
steps.how: The first real crop comes at about 30 months. Pick berries a few days after they turn fully blue, rolling them off gently with the thumb. Net the bushes against birds.

ways.note: Bushes usually give their first real berries at about 30 months (900 days).

mistakes: Planting in ordinary garden soil that is not sour enough, so the leaves turn yellow and the plant dies.
Trying to grow them in the hot lowlands.
Adding lime, ash or manure as for other crops.
Planting a single type, so few berries set.
better: Grow only in cool highlands and test the soil pH before planting.
Buy low chill types bred for warm places from a nursery you trust.
Raise native ayusip from cuttings instead of digging plants from the wild.
Keep records of flowering and fruiting. There is little local experience yet.

watering.traditional: The few blueberry growers in the highlands keep the beds or pots evenly damp, with rain water where they can, under a thick pine needle mulch. Wild ayusip lives on mountain rain.
watering.method: A watering can with rain water on the bed or pot, in the morning. Hard tap water slowly makes the soil less sour.
watering.rainfed: Plant as the rains begin and keep a thick pine needle mulch. In the misty highlands rain and fog carry the bushes much of the year, with hand watering in dry weeks. Rain water also keeps the soil sour, which blueberry needs.
watering.dryseason: Every day or two, more often for pots. Water when the top of the bed or pot feels dry or the young leaves droop.
watering.wet: Blueberry roots rot in standing water: use raised beds or pots that drain freely, and never let water pool.

schedule.often: Every day or two in dry weather. Pots may need water every day
schedule.amount: Enough to wet the whole root ball, never soggy
schedule.why: Blueberry roots are shallow, fine and without root hairs, so they dry out fast.

schedule.often: Whenever the top of the bed or pot is dry, a little often rather than a lot at once
schedule.amount: About 2.5 to 4 cm of water a week in total in dry weather
schedule.why: Steady damp soil grows the new canes that will bear.

schedule.stage: Flowering and berry growth to harvest
schedule.often: Keep evenly damp. Pots every day in dry, sunny weeks
schedule.amount: About 2.5 to 4 cm of water a week in total
schedule.why: Thirst while berries grow gives small, few berries.

critical: The first two months after planting.
Berry growth, from flowering to picking.

signs.dry: Young leaves droop, leaf edges turn brown and dry, and berries stay small.
signs.wet: Yellow leaves, dying roots and a sour smell in a bed or pot that does not drain.

better: Water a little and often with rain water under a thick pine needle mulch, so the shallow roots stay evenly damp.
